summary.text: For \(p\ge19\), quadratic reciprocity provides a square root \(r\) of \(5\bmod p\); choosing its sign so that \(r\) is even and \(6\le r\le p-6\), then setting \(m=r-4\), gives \(m^2+8m+11=pc\) with \(c\) odd and \(c\le m\). An explicit left-factorial formula for the continued fraction shows that \(2c\) cancels from its numerator and denominator, while size bounds prevent \(p\) from dividing the remaining denominator, leaving reduced numerator \(p\); the exceptional case \(p=11\) is evaluated directly.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad(2\le k<n-1),
\]
with terminal value
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is \(1/R_2(n)\). If \(R_2(n)=N/D\) in lowest terms, then \(1/R_2(n)=D/N\), so
\[
a(n)=|N|.
\]
We shall first derive a closed form for \(R_2(n)\), and then choose \(n\) so that the reduced numerator in that closed form is the prescribed prime.

Define the left-factorial sums
\[
G(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}i!,
\]
so that \(G(0)=0\) and
\[
G(t+1)=G(t)+t!.
\]
Two elementary properties of these sums will be used. First, \(G\) is nondecreasing. Second,
\[
2\mid G(t)\qquad(t\ge2).
\]
Indeed, \(0!+1!=2\), while every \(i!\) with \(i\ge2\) is even.

Write \(n=m+3\), where \(m\ge0\), and put
\[
M=m^2+8m+11.
\]
For integers \(j\ge0\), define
\[
Q_j=M\bigl(j(G(m+1)-G(j))+j!\bigr)
      -(m+3)(m+1)!j.
\]
A direct use of
\(G(j+1)=G(j)+j!\) and \((j+1)!=(j+1)j!\) gives the recurrence
\[
Q_{j+2}=(j+2)(Q_{j+1}-Q_j).                 \tag{1}
\]

We also need that
\[
Q_j>0\qquad(0\le j\le m+1).                 \tag{2}
\]
Here is the proof. If \(j=m+1\), then \(G(m+1)-G(j)=0\), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{m+1}
 &= (m+1)!\bigl(M-(m+3)(m+1)\bigr)\\
 &= (m+1)!(4m+8)>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(j\le m\), monotonicity of \(G\), together with
\(G(m+1)=G(m)+m!\), gives
\[
G(m+1)-G(j)\ge m!.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_j
&\ge M(jm!+j!)-(m+3)(m+1)!j\\
&=jm!\bigl(M-(m+3)(m+1)\bigr)+Mj!\\
&=jm!(4m+8)+Mj!>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (2), including \(j=0\), because the final term \(Mj!\) is positive.

We now claim that for \(0\le j\le m\),
\[
R_{j+2}(m+3)=(j+2)\frac{Q_j}{Q_{j+1}}.       \tag{3}
\]
We prove this by descending induction on \(j\). At \(j=m\), the left side is the terminal value
\[
R_{m+2}(m+3)=(m+2)+\frac{m+3}{4}=\frac{5m+11}{4}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
Q_m=(m+1)m!(5m+11)
\]
and
\[
Q_{m+1}=4(m+1)!(m+2),
\]
so
\[
(m+2)\frac{Q_m}{Q_{m+1}}=\frac{5m+11}{4}.
\]
Thus (3) holds at the terminal index.

Suppose it holds at \(j+1\). Since all the relevant \(Q\)'s are positive, no denominator below vanishes. Using the recursive definition of \(R\), the induction hypothesis, and (1), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{j+2}(m+3)
 &= (j+2)-\frac{j+3}{R_{j+3}(m+3)}\\
 &= (j+2)-\frac{Q_{j+2}}{Q_{j+1}}\\
 &= (j+2)-(j+2)\frac{Q_{j+1}-Q_j}{Q_{j+1}}\\
 &= (j+2)\frac{Q_j}{Q_{j+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (3).

Taking \(j=0\), we have \(Q_0=M\). Also, since \(G(1)=1\),
\[
Q_1=MG(m+1)-(m+3)(m+1)!.
\]
Therefore
\[
R_2(m+3)
 =\frac{2M}{MG(m+1)-(m+3)(m+1)!}.           \tag{4}
\]
Notice also from (2) that the denominator displayed in (4), which is \(Q_1\), is positive.

We next prove the number-theoretic part of the argument. Let \(p\) be a prime satisfying
\[
p\equiv1\pmod {10}\quad\hbox{or}\quad p\equiv9\pmod {10}.
\]
We first dispose of \(p=11\). For \(n=3\),
\[
R_2(3)=2+\frac34=\frac{11}{4},
\]
so the original continued fraction is \(4/11\), and therefore
\[
a(3)=11.
\]

We may henceforth assume \(p\ne11\). A prime in one of the two stated residue classes, other than \(11\), is at least \(19\). In particular, \(p\) is odd and \(p\ne5\).

We claim that \(5\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\). By quadratic reciprocity, because \(5\equiv1\pmod4\),
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right).
\]
The given congruence modulo \(10\) implies that \(p\equiv1\) or \(4\pmod5\). Both residues are squares modulo \(5\): they are respectively \(1^2\) and \(2^2\). Hence \((5/p)=1\), and there is a residue \(y\) modulo \(p\) such that
\[
y^2\equiv5\pmod p.                          \tag{5}
\]

For a residue class \(z\) modulo \(p\), let its value mean its least representative in \(\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}\). We can select from the two roots \(y\) and \(-y\) a root whose value is even. Indeed, if the value of \(y\) is even, use \(y\). Otherwise, \(y\ne0\), and the value of \(-y\) is \(p-y\). Both \(p\) and the value of \(y\) are then odd, so \(p-y\) is even.

Let \(z\) be the chosen root and let
\[
r\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}
\]
be its even value. Thus
\[
r^2\equiv5\pmod p.                          \tag{6}
\]
We need bounds on \(r\). Any least representative of a square root of \(5\) modulo a prime \(p\ge19\) is at least \(6\). For if it were one of \(0,1,2,3,4,5\), then \(p\) would divide one of
\[
-5,-4,-1,4,11,20,
\]
respectively. No prime at least \(19\) divides any of these integers. Applying the same observation to \(-z\), whose value is \(p-r\) because \(z\ne0\), gives
\[
r\ge6,
\qquad p-r\ge6.                              \tag{7}
\]
In particular,
\[
r+6\le p.                                   \tag{8}
\]

Set
\[
m=r-4.
\]
Then \(m\ge2\), \(m\) is even, and (8) says
\[
m+10\le p.                                  \tag{9}
\]
Moreover,
\[
M=m^2+8m+11=(m+4)^2-5=r^2-5.
\]
By (6), \(p\mid M\). Hence there is a positive integer \(c\) such that
\[
M=m^2+8m+11=pc.                              \tag{10}
\]
Positivity follows because \(r\ge6\), so \(r^2-5>0\).

We record two important properties of \(c\). First, \(c\) is odd. Since \(m\) is even,
\[
m^2+8m+11
\]
is odd; and since \(p\) is odd, (10) forces \(c\) to be odd.

Second,
\[
c\le m.                                     \tag{11}
\]
If instead \(c\ge m+1\), then by (9)
\[
pc\ge(m+10)(m+1)=m^2+11m+10.
\]
But for \(m\ge2\),
\[
m^2+11m+10>m^2+8m+11=M,
\]
contradicting (10).

We now analyze the cancellation in (4). Since \(m\ge2\), the elementary parity property of \(G\) gives an integer \(A\) such that
\[
G(m+1)=2A.                                   \tag{12}
\]
Also, \(2\mid m!\), and (11), together with \(c>0\), gives \(c\mid m!\). Since \(c\) is odd, \(2\) and \(c\) are coprime, so
\[
2c\mid m!.
\]
It follows in particular that
\[
2c\mid(m+3)(m+1)!.
\]
Thus there is an integer \(B\ge0\) such that
\[
(m+3)(m+1)!=2cB.                             \tag{13}
\]

Substituting (10), (12), and (13) into the denominator in (4) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
MG(m+1)-(m+3)(m+1)!
 &=pc\cdot2A-2cB\\
 &=2c(pA-B).
\end{aligned}                                \tag{14}
\]
This denominator is \(Q_1\), which was proved positive. Since \(2c>0\), (14) shows that
\[
pA-B>0.                                     \tag{15}
\]
Using (10) and (14), formula (4) now becomes
\[
R_2(m+3)=\frac{2pc}{2c(pA-B)}
         =\frac{p}{pA-B}.                    \tag{16}
\]

It remains essential to show that no further cancellation removes \(p\). We claim
\[
\gcd(p,pA-B)=1.                              \tag{17}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, failure of (17) would imply
\(p\mid pA-B\), and hence \(p\mid B\). Equation (13) would then give
\[
p\mid(m+3)(m+1)!.
\]
By primality, either \(p\mid m+3\) or \(p\mid(m+1)!\). The first alternative is impossible because (9) implies
\[
0<m+3<p.
\]
The second is also impossible: a prime dividing \((m+1)!\) must be at most \(m+1\), whereas (9) gives \(p\ge m+10\). This proves (17).

Therefore the right side of (16) is already in lowest terms, with positive denominator by (15), and its numerator is exactly \(p\). Since the continued fraction defining the sequence is the reciprocal of \(R_2(m+3)\), its reduced denominator is exactly \(p\). In other words,
\[
a(m+3)=p.
\]
The constructed index can also be written \(m+3=r-1\).

Combining this construction for every admissible prime \(p\ne11\) with the direct calculation \(a(3)=11\), we conclude that for every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\), there exists an index \(n\) such that \(a(n)=p\), as required.
